w: An iron lattice tower begun in Wembley Park by railway magnate Sir Edward Watkin, who wanted a 358-metre 'Great Tower of London' to outdo the Eiffel Tower. Only the first stage was ever finished; the half-built folly was demolished in 1907, and Wembley Stadium now stands on its footprint.
s: Unfinished Victorian folly meant to beat the Eiffel Tower
_facts: Planned height of 358m (1,175 ft), taller than the Eiffel Tower
Led by railway entrepreneur Sir Edward Watkin
Only partially built; demolished in 1907
Site later occupied by Wembley Stadium

w: A public park in Edgware that survives from a former country estate; St Lawrence's Church, the parish church of Little Stanmore, still stands here alongside the Chandos Mausoleum. The grounds now form a green pocket of the London Borough of Harrow, and give the surrounding residential area its name.
s: Country-estate remnant with a mausoleum and parish church
_facts: Once part of the Canons country estate
Contains St Lawrence's Church, parish church of Little Stanmore
Also holds the Chandos Mausoleum

w: A transport cafe beside the North Circular Road that became a shrine of British motorcycle culture after opening in 1938. It closed in 1969 but reopened on the same site in 1997, and bikers still gather here for meets and functions, the road's roar just outside the door.
_facts: Opened 1938, closed 1969, reopened 1997 on the original site
Located next to the North Circular Road
Historically significant venue in UK motorcycle culture

w: A working astronomical observatory tucked into suburban Northolt, quietly tracking near-Earth asteroids. Its follow-up astrometry of newly discovered small Solar System objects feeds into the global effort to chart hazardous rocks passing near Earth - serious science out of an ordinary London suburb.
s: Suburban observatory that tracks near-Earth asteroids
_facts: Collects follow-up astrometry of near-Earth asteroids
Contributes data on small Solar System objects

w: A purpose-built Sunni mosque on Station Road, opened in 2011 to replace a house-based mosque that had served the same street since 1985. It stands beside Harrow Civic Centre, just south of Wealdstone town centre, as the borough's main Islamic community hub.
_facts: Current building opened 2011 at 34 Station Road
Replaced a house-mosque at no. 36 Station Road, used from 1985
Adjacent to Harrow Civic Centre

w: A former St Andrew's Presbyterian church on Ealing Road, converted into the principal mosque of North West London. Together with the adjoining Muslim Welfare Association it holds up to 2,200 worshippers, serving a Pakistani and Bangladeshi community that makes up the UK's fifth largest Muslim population.
s: Former Presbyterian church, now Wembley's main mosque
_facts: Formerly St Andrew's Presbyterian Church
Holds up to 2,200 people with the adjoining Muslim Welfare Association
Serves the UK's fifth largest Muslim community

n: St Mary's, Harrow on the Hill
w: The Borough and Parish Church of Harrow on the Hill, sitting at the top of the hill from which the town takes its name. It holds Grade I listed status, marking it as a building of exceptional national interest amid the streets of this northwest London hilltop settlement.
s: Grade I parish church atop Harrow on the Hill
_facts: Borough and Parish Church of Harrow on the Hill
Church of England building
Grade I listed

w: A 76-acre Local Nature Reserve on the former grounds of the 18th-century Warren House mansion, passed to Harrow council in 1976 after stints with Middlesex County Council and the Greater London Council. Ancient woodland survives here, and muntjac deer, foxes and tawny owls are regularly seen.
s: Ancient woodland reserve on a lost 18th-century estate
_facts: 30.7 hectares (76 acres), a Local Nature Reserve
Once part of the grounds of the 18th-century Warren House mansion
Contains ancient woodland with wild service trees and hornbeam
Home to muntjac deer, tawny owls, kestrels and sparrowhawks

w: A footbridge into Wembley Stadium named after a police horse called Billy, who helped clear the pitch when up to 300,000 spectators spilled onto it before the first Wembley FA Cup Final in 1923. Though grey, Billy looked white in newsreels of the day; the current bridge, opened 2008, replaced the old crossing.
s: Bridge named after the horse that cleared 1923's pitch chaos
_facts: Named after police horse Billy, used at the chaotic 1923 FA Cup Final
Up to 200,000-300,000 spectators spilled onto the pitch that day
Replaced an older footbridge built for the British Empire Exhibition
Opened 2008, designed by Marks Barfield

w: The pedestrian road linking Wembley Park station to the stadium, built for the 1948 Olympics after Wembley's owners paid 120,000 pounds for direct Underground access. Work began in 1947, and the 500-yard carriageway was completed partly by German prisoners of war still held in Britain.
s: 1948 Olympics road partly built by German POWs
_facts: Built for the 1948 Summer Olympics
500 yards long, 45 feet wide
Constructed partly by German prisoners of war
Cost 120,000 pounds, funded by Wembley's owners
